items.rawSummary: Iran lifted airspace restrictions and flight operations are returning to normal after both sides paused strikes following President Trump's call for a ceasefire, with Tehran warning of broader retaliation if Israel strikes Lebanon again.
items.analysis: Israeli airstrikes struck military targets, a petrochemical facility, and an IRGC camp in Iran, while Iran launched ballistic missiles that were all intercepted. Following President Trump's call for a ceasefire, Iran's Khatam al-Anbiya Central Headquarters announced a halt to hostilities, though the IRGC warned of a stronger response if Israel strikes Lebanon; Israel paused its own strikes at Trump's request. The U.S. did not participate in offensive operations or shield Israel from missiles, according to CBS, contradicting earlier claims of U.S. involvement in interceptions, which the IDF described as limited to defensive roles. Iran subsequently lifted its airspace closure and began restoring normal flight operations, signaling a step toward de-escalation alongside the ceasefire. Separately, Expediency Council chief Sadeq Amoli Larijani warned that aggression against Iran's allies will now draw responses beyond regional borders, calling the recent missile strikes a new strategic doctrine, and the Iranian Army declared that the U.S. will bear responsibility for future Israeli aggression. Markets rallied on the ceasefire and talk of a 'final deal.'

items.rawSummary: Major earthquake in southern Philippines triggers Pacific tsunami alerts
items.analysis: A powerful earthquake struck the southern Philippines on June 7, with preliminary magnitude estimates ranging from 8.2 to 9.0. The Pacific Tsunami Warning Center issued a tsunami alert for the Philippines, Indonesia, Palau, Taiwan, and Papua New Guinea, warning that widespread hazardous waves are possible. Philippine authorities ordered evacuations in some coastal areas amid the threat. The event triggered rapid international alerts and precautionary measures across a broad region of the Pacific.

items.title: Strait of Hormuz area (Bandar Abbas vicinity), Iran: Bloomberg reported that the UK and France have a demining mission for the Strait of Hormuz ready, and allied leaders will seek President Trump's sign-off at the G7, with deployment following any Iran deal.
items.description: Bloomberg reported that the UK and France have a demining mission for the Strait of Hormuz ready, and allied leaders will seek President Trump's sign-off at the G7, with deployment following any Iran deal.
items.rawSummary: Conflicting Iranian statements indicate the Strait of Hormuz is both open under new transit fees and sealed, while the U.S. maintains a blockade, shipping rates surge, and the UK and France prepare a demining mission pending G7 approval.
items.analysis: Conflicting signals from Iran complicate the picture: its ambassador to Moscow said the Strait of Hormuz will stay open under new terms with Oman and transit fees, but Mehr News Agency reported Tehran has sealed off the strait and Bab el-Mandeb, with a source close to Parliament Speaker Ghalibaf threatening strikes on oil infrastructure in U.S.-allied Gulf states as retaliation for an Israeli strike on Mahshahr's petrochemical complex. The IRGC Navy has warned that any hostile combat vessel entering the strait will be targeted on sight. The U.S. blockade has redirected 132 commercial vessels and disabled six, while container spot rates from Asia to the U.S. West Coast have jumped 20% over the past week and Asia-to-Northern Europe rates 27%. Bloomberg reports that the UK and France have prepared a demining mission for the Strait of Hormuz, with allied leaders planning to seek President Trump's approval at the G7, to be deployed following any Iran deal—a sign that diplomatic efforts toward an off-ramp are advancing. Meanwhile, the Kalshi prediction market prices only a 31% chance of normalization by September, and a European official warns of possible escalation from Israeli actions in Lebanon.

items.title: Nearby Iranian positions (implied operational area), Iran: Iran reopened its airspace and all flights resumed, with operations returning to normal.
items.description: Iran reopened its airspace and all flights resumed, with operations returning to normal.
items.rawSummary: Following overnight Israeli strikes on military targets in Iran, a conditional pause took hold on June 8, with Iran reopening its airspace and resuming flights by late afternoon even as both sides traded warnings that calm remained fragile.
items.analysis: Nuclear negotiations between the U.S. and Iran collapsed earlier this week after leaked sticking points showed Iran refused to transfer enriched uranium out of the country, demanded total sanctions relief, and sought to exclude nuclear issues entirely; continued U.S. interception of Iranian ships and Israeli operations in Lebanon further strained the talks. The U.S. naval blockade has tightened dramatically, with Kpler data showing Iranian crude and condensate exports collapsed to 209,000 barrels per day in May, and U.S. Central Command reporting 132 commercial vessels redirected and 6 disabled in support of the blockade. On the morning of June 8, Israel launched coordinated strikes on military targets in Iran using air force and navy assets, with air-launched ballistic missiles fired from Iraqi airspace; the IRGC confirmed the strikes hit air defense systems and ballistic missile sites, and they appeared notably smaller than previous waves and were carried out without U.S. aerial refueling support. Hours later, the Israeli military announced the Chief of General Staff was commanding operations from the air force command center, while U.S. Senator Chris Murphy asserted that Trump has lost control of the war and that Israel retaliated despite being told not to; a claim that the strikes were coordinated with the United States directly contradicts those assertions, suggesting Washington may have been more involved than initially acknowledged. Anti-aircraft fire and explosions were subsequently reported in Tehran, Karaj, and Isfahan, with smoke rising in the mountains east of Tehran and a petrochemical plant in Mahshahr still burning from earlier hits. Iran International reported that Iran's leadership lost contact with Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei the previous night and that the prior day's retaliatory strikes on Israel were launched without coordination with his office, relying on pre-prepared military protocols and suggesting a breakdown in command during the escalation. Iran's Khatam al-Anbiya Headquarters then announced a halt to military operations against Israel while warning of a much stronger response if attacks in southern Lebanon continue; Israel and the U.S. reportedly told Iran there would be no further attacks if Iran does not launch more strikes, a conditional pause pointing to efforts on both sides to contain the immediate escalation. Domestic disruption intensified through the day, with all flights cancelled and Iranian airspace closed, though by late afternoon Iran reopened its airspace and all flight operations returned to normal, a move signaling some stabilization after the overnight strikes. By afternoon, Prime Minister Netanyahu publicly framed the overnight strikes as historic action to prevent a nuclear attack on Israel, declared that Iran will not acquire a nuclear weapon, and warned the campaign is not over, while Iran's National Security Council Secretary responded that the region would "become hell" for the coalition if it errs, and parliamentary speaker Ghalibaf dismissed the viability of paper ceasefire agreements, signaling that the pause remains deeply fragile.

The U.S. naval blockade has tightened dramatically, with Kpler data showing Iranian crude and condensate exports collapsed to 209,000 barrels per day in May, and U.S. Central Command reporting 132 commercial vessels redirected and 6 disabled in support of the blockade. On the morning of June 8, Israel launched coordinated strikes on military targets in Iran using air force and navy assets, with air-launched ballistic missiles fired from Iraqi airspace; the IRGC confirmed the strikes hit air defense systems and ballistic missile sites, and they appeared notably smaller than previous waves and were carried out without U.S. aerial refueling support. Hours later, the Israeli military announced the Chief of General Staff was commanding operations from the air force command center, while U.S. Senator Chris Murphy asserted that Trump has lost control of the war and that Israel retaliated despite being told not to; a claim that the strikes were coordinated with the United States directly contradicts those assertions, suggesting Washington may have been more involved than initially acknowledged. Anti-aircraft fire and explosions were subsequently reported in Tehran, Karaj, and Isfahan, with smoke rising in the mountains east of Tehran and a petrochemical plant in Mahshahr still burning from earlier hits. Iran International reported that Iran's leadership lost contact with Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei the previous night and that the prior day's retaliatory strikes on Israel were launched without coordination with his office, relying on pre-prepared military protocols and suggesting a breakdown in command during the escalation. Iran's Khatam al-Anbiya Headquarters then announced a halt to military operations against Israel while warning of a much stronger response if attacks in southern Lebanon continue; Israel and the U.S. reportedly told Iran there would be no further attacks if Iran does not launch more strikes, a conditional pause pointing to efforts on both sides to contain the immediate escalation. Domestic disruption intensified through the day, with all flights cancelled and Iranian airspace closed, though by late afternoon Iran reopened its airspace and all flight operations returned to normal, a move signaling some stabilization after the overnight strikes. By afternoon, Prime Minister Netanyahu publicly framed the overnight strikes as historic action to prevent a nuclear attack on Israel, declared that Iran will not acquire a nuclear weapon, and warned the campaign is not over, while Iran's National Security Council Secretary responded that the region would "become hell" for the coalition if it errs, and parliamentary speaker Ghalibaf dismissed the viability of paper ceasefire agreements, signaling that the pause remains deeply fragile.
items.keyPoint: Netanyahu warned that Israel's campaign against Iran and Hezbollah is not over and threatened a forceful response to any renewed Iranian attacks.
